name: Carmine
lede: Carmine is a deep red with a slight blue cast, named for the lake made from scale insects, first kermes and then the Mexican cochineal; the same insect still colors lipstick, yogurt and Campari.

sections.title: A word from a worm
sections.body:
Carmine and [[crimson]] are cousins, and both go back to the kermes insect. Ball and Coles both name kermes as the source of the English words crimson and carmine, and of the French *cramoisi* [1][2]. Finlay traces carmine to a Sanskrit name for the insect and notes that Persian speakers still use *kermes* when they want to say red [3].

For the first dyers the insect was a mystery. Theophrastus called the dried bodies *kokkos*, a berry, because the insects look like berries clustered on a twig [1]. Paterson's dictionary describes carmine as an old red, orange or crimson pigment that came first from the kermes insect and later from the cochineal [4].

Carmine was a material before it was a hue name. To a medieval or Renaissance painter it meant a lake made from scale insects, and the word *lake*, now a generic label for dye-based pigments, once meant red alone [1][5].

sections.title: The cochineal
sections.body:
The insect that made carmine famous is the cochineal, *Dactylopius coccus*, which lives on prickly pear cactus in Mexico and South America [6]. The dye is carminic acid, which the female insect makes to deter predators [7][8]. The Pigment Compendium lists it as a complex acid with three fused carbon rings, a dark purplish-brown mass or a bright red powder, and indexes it as Colour Index 75470 [8].

It is a remarkably strong dye: St Clair says the color from a pound of farmed cochineal is said to equal that of ten or twelve pounds of kermes [6]. The price was the number of insects. St Clair puts a pound of dried raw cochineal at around 70,000 bodies, while Coles says some 14,000 insects go into 100 grams of carmine lake pigment [6][7]. The counts differ because they measure different products, a raw dye against a finished pigment, and the safest statement is that it took tens of thousands.

sections.title: Aztecs, Spain and the secret crop
sections.body:
The dye was in use in the Americas long before Europeans arrived [7][6]. Coles dates its use for textiles to about 700 BCE, while St Clair says at least the second century BCE; books disagree, but both place it deep in the pre-Columbian past [7][6]. St Clair cites an Aztec tribute list from about 1520 that required the Mixtec people to give 40 sacks of cochineal a year and the Zapotecs 20 bags every 80 days [6].

Color marked rank. Captain Baltasar de Ocampo, who watched the execution of the last royal Inca, Túpac Amaru, in 1572, described him in a crimson velvet mantle and doublet [6]. Spain soon made the dye part of its empire's income. One observer wrote that in 1587 alone, about 144,000 pounds of cochineal, roughly 72 tons, left Lima for Spain [6]. Our library dates the beginning of Spanish imports to about 1520 [10].

Spain guarded the source. Until the eighteenth century the dye had by law to land at Seville or Cádiz, from where it went on to color Venetian velvets from the mid-sixteenth century and to help fund the Dutch dye industry [6]. Finlay tells of rival attempts to grow the cactus elsewhere, among them Dr James Anderson's plantation of prickly pears in Madras in the 1780s, an English experiment that was mostly abandoned [3].

sections.title: Dye, mordant and lake
sections.body:
Carmine is not simply crushed insect. The dye needs a mordant to hold it, usually alum, and the other additives, acids or metals such as tin, shift the result anywhere between pale pink and a red that is nearly black [6]. Field wrote in 1835 that the crimson and scarlet colors from cochineal come from the action of tin [5].

A painter needs the color as a solid, so the dye is turned into a lake. Coles describes the method: the ground insects are simmered in water, the liquid is mixed with alum and cream of tartar, soda ash is added so that a pigment precipitates, and the solid settles overnight [2]. Colourmen then sold it under many names. Carlyle lists carmine, crimson lake, crimson lake extra and extra carmine lake, and mixes of vermilion with carmine had names of their own [5].

The word spread past its source. Field noted that carmine was originally given only to lakes of cochineal or kermes, then to any pigment as rich and fine, so that people spoke of blue carmines [5]. Indigo carmine is the best known: Balfour-Paul says a method invented in 1740 mixed ground indigo with sulphuric acid to make bright turquoise-blue dyes, and a late nineteenth-century German source judged indigo carmine the most suitable dye for ink [11].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
For centuries carmine was one of the painter's costly reds. Gage records Le Blon's early three-color printing, for which he needed a red made from a complicated mixture of madder lake, carmine and a little natural cinnabar [12]. A later palette diagram shows carmine set beside Naples yellow and ultramarine in a flesh-painting set [12]. Van Gogh's own palette sketch of 1882 ran from white to vermilion, and he said that ultramarine, carmine and the like were added only when strictly necessary [12].

Carmine also faded, and the clearest case is Turner [13]. Finlay reports that the carmine on Turner's *Waves Breaking against the Wind* has largely disappeared and that he bought the pigment, made from cochineal, from London suppliers [13][3]. A Tate conservator says that Winsor, of the paint firm Winsor and Newton, objected to some of the pigments Turner bought [13]. Gurney's modern list of historic or not recommended pigments still names carmine red [14].

Carmine also hides in the old color systems. The Werner and Syme list of reds includes carmine red, and Schäffer's red list had carmine, along with kugellack and Florentine lake, which Baty describes as variants of it [15][16]. Baty adds that pigment names alone were no guarantee, since early pigments were often adulterated [16].

sections.title: Food, lips and Campari
sections.body:
Cochineal outlived the painter's paintbox. Greenfield explains that making carminic acid in a laboratory is too complex to pay, so the insects remain the only commercially viable source of the dye [9]. On European labels it appears as additive E120, as cochineal extract, as carmine, or simply as coloring added, and it is found in candy, yogurt, sausages, fruit juice, cough syrup, lipstick, eyeshadow and Campari [9].

Lipstick shows the naming habit. Pastoureau notes that once lip color became a mass-market product in tubes, carmine, garnet, cherry, vermilion and poppy were not enough, and the shades were given catchy phrases instead [17]. Greenfield points out that the name of Mérimée's heroine Carmen, from his novella of 1845, is close to the French word for the cochineal's color [18].

sections.title: Blood, bugs and the number of insects
sections.body:
Finlay writes that carmine is made of blood. It is better to say it is made of an insect: the dye is carminic acid, a compound made by the female cochineal, and it sits in the insect's body [13][7][8]. Readers who see the colorant on a food label are seeing that insect.

The story that carmine was always the same red is also wrong. Early carmine came from kermes, which is weaker, and the bright cochineal version only reached European workshops after the Spanish conquest [3][10]. The counts of insects per pound vary between books, so we say tens of thousands and no more [6][7].

sections.title: What the swatch shows
sections.body:
The swatch here, #960018, is a deep, slightly bluish red, the value our library takes from Wikipedia's listing, and ISCC-NBS calls the nearest block a deep red [10]. It is not a measurement of any particular lake. Ridgway's 1912 plate is greyer and browner, and RAL 3003 is a slightly greyer, bluer red [10].

A carmine paint varied from cool crimson to nearly black, depending on mordant and thickness, and it faded in light [6][13]. A screen swatch cannot show that. Think of the swatch as the standard color the name has come to mean.

Its nearest named neighbors in our library are [[falu-red]] at a distance of 4.3 CIEDE2000 units, then Oxheart at 5.7 and [[maroon]] at 6.0, each duller or darker [10]. Beside [[crimson]] it is darker and less blue, and beside [[scarlet]] and [[vermilion]] it is cooler and deeper [10]. A useful test for the eye is to look at the red cap or robe in a fifteenth-century portrait and ask whether it leans toward blue, as carmine does, or toward orange, as vermilion does.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, 107 contain a color within six CIEDE2000 units of this swatch covering at least 5 per cent of the canvas, as photographed [19]. They cluster in one century. In the 1400s the rate is 5.4 times the archive average: 23 of 945 paintings [19]. The 1480s are the peak, with 9 of 141 paintings, 14 times the archive rate [19].

Hans Memling stands out, with 3 of his 19 paintings in the archive, a rate about 35 times the average [19]. The biggest areas are in an anonymous [[painting:nga-46153|Portrait of an Ecclesiastic]] of 1480, where it covers over a third of the canvas, in a portrait of a young man in a red cap attributed to [[painter:sandro-botticelli|Botticelli]], and in his [[painting:nga-41671|Giuliano de' Medici]] [19].

This needs a caveat. Spanish imports of cochineal began about 1520, so these Renaissance reds cannot be Mexican cochineal [10]. They may be kermes or lac lakes, or vermilion, and photographs of aged, varnished paintings cannot say which [19]. The match is a color, not a pigment test. In a wider count, the color most often plays an accent inside the painting, in 89 per cent of 157 paintings [19]. The word *carmine* peaked in printed English around the 1890s, and by 2000 it was at about a fifth of that level [19].
